SEVERANCE OF A JOINT TENANCY (CIV. CODE §§ 683, 683.2; PROB. CODE § 5042; RIDDLE V. HARMON; TENHET V. BOSWELL; ESTATE OF PROPST) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for the residence at 1234 Elm Street, Sacramento, California · Frances P. Riddle

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's rules on how a joint tenancy is severed — what a joint tenancy is and what the right of survivorship means; the common-law and statutory rule that any one joint tenant may sever the joint tenancy as to that tenant's own interest without the consent of the others; the specific written means of severance and the recording requirement that Civil Code section 683.2 attaches to real property; the Court of Appeal's holding in Riddle v. Harmon that a joint tenant may sever by a deed to himself or herself without an intermediary; the California Supreme Court's holdings in Tenhet v. Boswell that a lease by one joint tenant does not sever the tenancy and that encumbrances a deceased joint tenant placed on the property do not bind the survivor, and in Estate of Propst that a joint tenancy in personal property may also be unilaterally severed; and the Probate Code rule that a dissolution of marriage severs a joint tenancy between former spouses — as background in connection with the property described as the residence at 1234 Elm Street, Sacramento, California, which is or was held in joint tenancy by Frances P. Riddle and Jack C. Riddle, in Sacramento County, California. It states what the statutes and the published opinions say. It does not state whether that joint tenancy has been severed, whether any particular instrument would sever it, or what any person should do.

WHAT A JOINT TENANCY IS: EXPRESS DECLARATION AND THE FOUR UNITIES
Civil Code section 683, subdivision (a), defines a joint interest as one owned by two or more persons in equal shares, by a title created by a single will or transfer, when expressly declared in the will or transfer to be a joint tenancy. The same subdivision lists the transfers that can create one directly — among them a transfer from a sole owner to himself or herself and others, from tenants in common or joint tenants to themselves or some of them or to themselves and others, and from spouses holding title as community property or otherwise to themselves or to themselves and others or to one of them and another — in each case when expressly declared in the transfer to be a joint tenancy, together with a grant or devise to executors or trustees as joint tenants. The California Supreme Court explained in Tenhet v. Boswell that this statute, requiring an express declaration for the creation of a joint interest, does not abrogate the common-law rule that four unities are essential to an estate in joint tenancy — unity of interest, unity of time, unity of title, and unity of possession — and that the four-unities requirement reflects the basic concept that there is but one estate taken jointly, so that if an essential unity is destroyed the joint tenancy is severed and a tenancy in common results. Tenhet also states that under Civil Code sections 683 and 686 a joint tenancy must be expressly declared in the creating instrument or a tenancy in common results, a statutory departure from the common-law preference in favor of joint tenancy.

THE RIGHT OF SURVIVORSHIP IS AN EXPECTANCY; ANY JOINT TENANT MAY SEVER UNILATERALLY
The principal feature of a joint tenancy is the right of survivorship — the jus accrescendi — and severance extinguishes it. The California Supreme Court, in a passage from Tenhet v. Boswell that it later repeated in Estate of Propst, describes a joint tenant's right of survivorship as an expectancy that is not irrevocably fixed upon the creation of the estate: it arises only upon success in the ultimate gamble — survival — and then only if the unity of the estate has not previously been destroyed by voluntary conveyance, by partition proceedings, by involuntary alienation under an execution, or by any other action which operates to sever the joint tenancy. Against that background, the Court of Appeal in Riddle v. Harmon states that an indisputable right of each joint tenant is the power to convey his or her separate estate, by way of gift or otherwise, without the knowledge or consent of the other joint tenant and thereby terminate the joint tenancy; Propst quotes that sentence as the rule California courts have consistently applied to real property. Propst also states the consequence: severance converts the joint tenancy into a tenancy in common, and because a tenant in common also holds an undivided fractional interest, a unilateral severance by one joint tenant does not deprive the other joint tenants of their fractional shares. What severance removes is the survivorship feature, not the co-owners' shares.

STATUTORY MEANS OF SEVERING A JOINT TENANCY IN REAL PROPERTY (CIV. CODE § 683.2(A))
Civil Code section 683.2, subdivision (a), lists the ways a joint tenant may sever a joint tenancy in real property as to that joint tenant's own interest without the joinder or consent of the other joint tenants. The list is stated to be subject to the limitations and requirements of the section and to be in addition to any other means by which a joint tenancy may be severed. The two enumerated means are: (1) execution and delivery of a deed that conveys legal title to the joint tenant's interest to a third person, whether or not under an agreement that requires the third person to reconvey legal title to the joint tenant; and (2) execution of a written instrument that evidences the intent to sever the joint tenancy — including a deed that names the joint tenant as transferee — or of a written declaration that, as to the interest of the joint tenant, the joint tenancy is severed. The California Supreme Court in Estate of Propst describes the section, enacted in 1984, as setting forth several means of severing a real property joint tenancy, including a severance by transfer of a joint tenant's interest to himself or herself, and notes that the statute itself expressly provides that its listed means of severance are not exclusive. The limitations the section places on these means — a written agreement of the joint tenants, and the recording requirement for a severance of record — are addressed in the following clauses.

RIDDLE V. HARMON: SEVERANCE BY A DEED TO ONESELF, WITHOUT AN INTERMEDIARY
In Riddle v. Harmon (1980), the Court of Appeal decided whether a joint tenant had unilaterally terminated a joint tenancy by conveying her interest from herself as joint tenant to herself as tenant in common. Mrs. Riddle and her husband held a parcel as joint tenants; several months before her death she learned from her estate-planning attorney that the property would pass to her husband on her death, and she asked that the joint tenancy be terminated so that she could dispose of her interest by will. The attorney prepared a grant deed by which she granted herself an undivided one-half interest, reciting that its purpose was to terminate the joint tenancies between her and her husband, together with a will disposing of that interest; both were executed on December 8, 1975, and she died twenty days later. The trial court quieted title in the husband. The Court of Appeal reversed. It recounted the common-law "two-to-transfer" notion, rooted in the feudal livery-of-seisin ceremony, that a person cannot be both grantor and grantee, and the earlier decision in Clark v. Carter (1968) that had treated a conveyance through a third-party "strawman" as indispensable; it observed that California had already abandoned the strawman requirement for creating a joint tenancy by amending Civil Code section 683, and that attorneys had developed circuitous devices — a strawman conveyance and reconveyance, or a transfer to a trustee — to accomplish unilateral termination. The court discarded the rule that one cannot enfeoff oneself, rejected the rationale of Clark, and held that one joint tenant may unilaterally sever the joint tenancy without the use of an intermediary device. The court's footnote adds that construing the deed as a termination results in a tenancy in common, consistent with California's statutory preference for recognizing tenancies in common. Civil Code section 683.2(a)(2), enacted four years later, now expressly lists a deed that names the joint tenant as transferee among the written instruments that can sever.

LIMIT: NO SEVERANCE CONTRARY TO A WRITTEN AGREEMENT OF THE JOINT TENANTS (CIV. CODE § 683.2(B))
Civil Code section 683.2, subdivision (b), states that nothing in the section authorizes severance of a joint tenancy contrary to a written agreement of the joint tenants. The same subdivision adds a protection for third parties: a severance made contrary to such a written agreement does not defeat the rights of a purchaser or encumbrancer for value in good faith and without knowledge of the written agreement. The statute does not describe what such an agreement must contain beyond being written and being an agreement of the joint tenants. The case law is consistent with this limit: the Supreme Court's holding in Estate of Propst that a joint tenancy in personal property may be unilaterally severed is expressly stated to apply in the absence of prior contrary agreement, and Tenhet v. Boswell notes that joint tenants who no longer wish to continue the joint tenancy might convert it into a tenancy in common by written mutual agreement.

RECORDING REQUIREMENT FOR A SEVERANCE OF RECORD (CIV. CODE § 683.2(C)-(E))
For a joint tenancy in real property that is of record, Civil Code section 683.2, subdivision (c), provides that a severance by deed, written declaration, or other written instrument under subdivision (a) is not effective to terminate the right of survivorship of the other joint tenants as to the severing joint tenant's interest unless one of two requirements is satisfied. The first, in paragraph (1), is that before the death of the severing joint tenant the deed, written declaration, or other written instrument effecting the severance is recorded in the county where the real property is located. The second, in paragraph (2), is a narrow alternative for an instrument executed shortly before death: the instrument is executed and acknowledged before a notary public by the severing joint tenant not earlier than three days before that joint tenant's death, and is recorded in the county where the real property is located not later than seven days after the severing joint tenant's death. Subdivision (d) states that nothing in subdivision (c) limits the manner or effect of three things: a written instrument executed by all the joint tenants that severs the joint tenancy; a severance made by or pursuant to a written agreement of all the joint tenants; and a deed from a joint tenant to another joint tenant. Subdivision (e) fixes the temporal reach of the section: subdivisions (a) and (b) apply to all joint tenancies in real property whether created before, on, or after January 1, 1985, except that where a joint tenant died before January 1, 1985, the validity of a severance under subdivisions (a) and (b) is determined by the law in effect at the time of death; and subdivisions (c) and (d) do not apply to or affect a severance made before January 1, 1986. For the property described as the residence at 1234 Elm Street, Sacramento, California in Sacramento County, the county of recording referred to in subdivision (c) is the county where that real property is located.

TENHET V. BOSWELL: A LEASE BY ONE JOINT TENANT DOES NOT SEVER; SEVERANCE REQUIRES A CLEAR AND UNAMBIGUOUS ACT
In Tenhet v. Boswell (1976), one of two joint tenants leased the joint tenancy property to a third person for a ten-year term, assertedly without the other joint tenant's knowledge or consent, and died about three months later. The California Supreme Court, after surveying centuries of conflicting academic authority on whether a lease severs a joint tenancy, concluded that a lease is not so inherently inconsistent with joint tenancy as to create a severance, either temporary or permanent. Its reasoning rested on the express-intent requirement: because under Civil Code sections 683 and 686 a joint tenancy arises only upon an express declaration, the court declined to find a severance in circumstances which do not clearly and unambiguously establish that either of the joint tenants desired to terminate the estate. The court catalogued the alternative and unambiguous means that were available: the joint tenants might have converted the estate into a tenancy in common by written mutual agreement, or jointly conveyed the property and divided the proceeds; and, even without agreement, either might have severed the joint tenancy, with or without the other's consent, by an act clearly indicative of an intent to terminate, such as a conveyance of his or her entire interest, or by bringing an action to partition the property, which upon judgment would have effected a severance. On that basis the court held that the lease did not operate to sever the joint tenancy, so that sole ownership vested in the surviving joint tenant on the lessor's death by operation of the right of survivorship.

The California Supreme Court, in a passage from Tenhet v. Harmon (1980), the Court of Appeal decided whether a joint tenant had unilaterally terminated a joint tenancy by conveying her interest from herself as joint tenant to herself as tenant in common. Mrs. Riddle and her husband held a parcel as joint tenants; several months before her death she learned from her estate-planning attorney that the property would pass to her husband on her death, and she asked that the joint tenancy be terminated so that she could dispose of her interest by will. The attorney prepared a grant deed by which she granted herself an undivided one-half interest, reciting that its purpose was to terminate the joint tenancies between her and her husband, together with a will disposing of that interest; both were executed on December 8, 1975, and she died twenty days later. The trial court quieted title in the husband. The Court of Appeal reversed. It recounted the common-law "two-to-transfer" notion, rooted in the feudal livery-of-seisin ceremony, that a person cannot be both grantor and grantee, and the earlier decision in Clark v. Carter (1968) that had treated a conveyance through a third-party "strawman" as indispensable; it observed that California had already abandoned the strawman requirement for creating a joint tenancy by amending Civil Code section 683, and that attorneys had developed circuitous devices — a strawman conveyance and reconveyance, or a transfer to a trustee — to accomplish unilateral termination. The court discarded the rule that one cannot enfeoff oneself, rejected the rationale of Clark, and held that one joint tenant may unilaterally sever the joint tenancy without the use of an intermediary device. The court's footnote adds that construing the deed as a termination results in a tenancy in common, consistent with California's statutory preference for recognizing tenancies in common. Civil Code section 683.2(a)(2), enacted four years later, now expressly lists a deed that names the joint tenant as transferee among the written instruments that can sever.

expectedJSON.body: In Tenhet v. Boswell (1976), one of two joint tenants leased the joint tenancy property to a third person for a ten-year term, assertedly without the other joint tenant's knowledge or consent, and died about three months later. The California Supreme Court, after surveying centuries of conflicting academic authority on whether a lease severs a joint tenancy, concluded that a lease is not so inherently inconsistent with joint tenancy as to create a severance, either temporary or permanent. Its reasoning rested on the express-intent requirement: because under Civil Code sections 683 and 686 a joint tenancy arises only upon an express declaration, the court declined to find a severance in circumstances which do not clearly and unambiguously establish that either of the joint tenants desired to terminate the estate. The court catalogued the alternative and unambiguous means that were available: the joint tenants might have converted the estate into a tenancy in common by written mutual agreement, or jointly conveyed the property and divided the proceeds; and, even without agreement, either might have severed the joint tenancy, with or without the other's consent, by an act clearly indicative of an intent to terminate, such as a conveyance of his or her entire interest, or by bringing an action to partition the property, which upon judgment would have effected a severance. On that basis the court held that the lease did not operate to sever the joint tenancy, so that sole ownership vested in the surviving joint tenant on the lessor's death by operation of the right of survivorship.

During the lessor's lifetime, the court explained, the lessor's interest was an undivided interest in fee simple that encompassed the right to lease, so that a lease by one joint tenant is valid insofar as the lessor's interest is concerned; but by the very nature of joint tenancy the interest of the nonsurviving joint tenant is extinguished upon death, and it follows that the lease of the joint tenancy property also expires when the lessor dies. The court found this conclusion borne out by earlier California decisions on liens and mortgages: Zeigler v. In Estate of Propst (1990), the California Supreme Court decided whether a joint tenancy in personal property, such as a joint tenancy bank account, may be severed by the unilateral action of one joint tenant. The decedent had withdrawn all the funds from bank accounts he held in joint tenancy with his wife and deposited them in accounts in his own name, intending to cut off her right of survivorship; the lower courts, following a line of earlier California decisions holding that proceeds of personal property held in joint tenancy retain their joint tenancy character even in one tenant's name, ruled that the funds still passed to the widow. The Supreme Court reversed, disapproved those earlier holdings, and held that in the absence of prior contrary agreement, joint tenancies in personal property, like joint tenancies in real property, may be unilaterally severed. The court gave its holding retroactive effect, subject to a limited exception: a party claiming a right of survivorship who proves reasonable reliance on the prior rule, and proves that applying the new rule would therefore cause that party substantial detriment, may have the right of survivorship enforced under the former rule; the resulting detriment must be substantial, and mere disappointment of expectations is insufficient.

Probate Code section 5042, subdivision (a), provides that, except as provided in subdivision (b), a joint tenancy between the decedent and the decedent's former spouse, created before or during the marriage or registered domestic partnership, is severed as to the decedent's interest if, at the time of the decedent's death, the former spouse is not the decedent's surviving spouse as defined in section 78, as a result of the dissolution or annulment of the marriage or registered domestic partnership. Subdivision (c) preserves the rights of a subsequent purchaser or encumbrancer for value in good faith who relies on an apparent severance under the section or who lacks knowledge of a severance under it. Subdivision (d) provides that, for purposes of the section, property held in "joint tenancy" includes property held as community property with right of survivorship as described in Civil Code section 682.1.
